questions.enonce_markdown:
To what extent can Ramadan be described as a "month among all months" in Islam?

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** Ramadan is the ninth month of the Islamic lunar calendar. Muslims hold that it is the most blessed month of the year, and the description "a month among all months" is easy to defend. It must still be remembered that other times are also honoured in Islam.

**1. The revelation of the Quran.** According to Surah al-Baqarah (2), the Quran was sent down in Ramadan as guidance for people. Muslims therefore recite and study it more in this month, and many complete a reading of the whole book. Surah al-Qadr (97) speaks of the Night of Power (Laylat al-Qadr), which it declares better than a thousand months, and Muslims look for it in the last ten nights of Ramadan.

**2. The fast (sawm).** Fasting in Ramadan is the fourth pillar of Islam. Every adult Muslim who is healthy and not travelling abstains from food, drink and marital relations from dawn to sunset. Surah al-Baqarah says that fasting was prescribed so that believers may become conscious of God (taqwa). The sick, travellers, the elderly, pregnant and nursing women may be exempted and make up the days or give food to the poor.

**3. Spiritual discipline and prayer.** Muslims say extra night prayers (taraweeh) in the mosque, give more charity, ask forgiveness and try to avoid quarrels and bad speech. Many spend the last ten days in retreat (itikaf) in the mosque. According to hadith, the gates of paradise are opened and sins are forgiven for those who fast with faith.

**4. Social effects.** Families break the fast together at sunset (iftar). The fast teaches self-control and makes the rich feel the hunger of the poor. Zakat al-Fitr is paid before the end of the month, and the month ends with the festival of Eid al-Fitr.

**5. Limits of the description.** Ramadan is not the only honoured time. Dhul-Hijjah, the month of the Hajj, contains the day of Arafat and Eid al-Adha; four months (Dhul-Qadah, Dhul-Hijjah, Muharram and Rajab) are described as sacred in Surah al-Tawbah (9); Friday is the best day of the week and the Night of Power is a single night. Moreover, Muslims do not worship the month itself but God, who ordained the fast.

**Conclusion.** To a very large extent Ramadan can be called a month among all months, because it combines the revelation of the Quran, a pillar of the faith and an intense spiritual life, though Islam also honours other months and days.
